Anchor.Text: Consensus calls the LLM at once

Applied.Outcome: No quiet period: the call starts the moment Send to LLM is pressed. Step 2 and QuietSeconds are removed.

Replies.Text: No. Consensus should invoke the LLM instantly.

Instantly, then: no quiet period. The call starts the moment a thread starts waiting on the LLM.

One thing stays: only one call runs at a time for a proposal. If you comment again while a call is still running, that comment is picked up by a second call as soon as the first ends. Two calls writing the same text at once would refuse each other with a stale revision.

Outcome: step 2 and `QuietSeconds` go; step 3 starts at once, one call per proposal at a time.

Anchor.Text: The LLM answers with one JSON object.
Anchor.Suffix: For each waiting thread, a repl

Applied.Outcome: No tools. The prompt carries the text, every thread and search results for each waiting thread; the LLM answers with one JSON object of replies and applies, which Consensus checks and carries out as the llm participant.

Replies.Text: If we already sending the latest revision of the proposal and the entire contested threads in the prompt, what good are the tools? I suppose the LLM may wish to retrieve different revisions or read non-contested threads. is this tools worth it?

Fair question, and I think the answer is no: the tools are not worth it.

What a call needs to *read* can be put in the prompt: the text, all the threads (not just the contested ones), and the top search results for each waiting thread, which Consensus can run itself. Older revisions are rarely needed; when one is, the LLM can say so in its reply.

What a call needs to *do* is only two things, reply and apply. Instead of tools, the LLM answers with one JSON object: for each thread, either a reply `{ Thread, Reply }` or an apply `{ Thread, Outcome, Text? }`, or nothing. Consensus checks it and makes the calls itself, with the same rules as now.

That drops the MCP server entirely. It also works the same with any model, including small Ollama models that are weak at calling tools but can follow a JSON format (Ollama can even enforce one).

The cost: the LLM gets one look and cannot go looking for more. For discussing one proposal I think that is enough.

Outcome: no tools; the prompt carries everything, the answer is one JSON object, Consensus carries it out.

Replies.Text: No. This might come in a saved batch or in response to a user action.

Understood. What starts a call is anything that leaves something waiting on the LLM: one reply, a saved batch of changes, or an action like a button press.

The one thing I would keep from that bullet is that the LLM's own replies and applies never start another call, so it cannot talk to itself in a loop.

One question: do you want an explicit action too, such as an **Ask the LLM** button on a proposal or thread, that starts a call even when nothing is waiting on it?

Outcome: the bullet becomes "Anything that leaves work waiting on the LLM starts a call; the LLM's own writes never do."

Anchor.Text: One more moving part in the server: the call itself.

Applied.Outcome: The moving part is the call itself: claude -p as a separate program for claude-cli, an HTTP request for ollama. There is no queue; the disabled button keeps calls from overlapping.

Replies.Text: This needs clarification.

In plainer words, and updated for the other threads:

* **The queue:** the server keeps a short list of proposals that need a call. It runs at most one call per proposal at a time. When one finishes and more is waiting, it runs the next.
* **The child process** only applies to `claude-cli`. Consensus starts `claude -p` as a separate program, hands it the prompt, and reads its answer when it exits. For `ollama` it is just an HTTP request.

Neither is much code: a list, a flag per proposal and one of two ways to send a prompt.

Outcome: the bullet is rewritten along these lines.

Applied.Outcome: Step 1 is now the Send to LLM button in the proposal heading; nothing else starts a call. The automatic trigger and the one-call-per-proposal queue are replaced by the button and its disabled state.

Replies.Text:
From Andre in the terminal: a **Send to LLM** button in the proposal heading, beside Comment on the whole document and Approve as Plan. It packages everything waiting on the LLM in this proposal and sends it in one call.

It follows an idea set aside: a Ctrl+L hotkey to push to the LLM *instead* of the automatic trigger. Read the same way, the button **replaces** the automatic trigger: replying, resolving and new threads no longer start a call; you work through the threads at your own pace and send when ready. That also settles the question of an Ask the LLM button.

What the button would do:

* It shows how many threads are waiting on the LLM, e.g. **Send to LLM (3)**, and is disabled at 0.
* While the call runs it reads **LLM working…** and cannot be pressed again; the replies appear live when it finishes.
* A failure shows on each thread it was for, as agreed.
* The package is what the tools thread settled on: the text, all threads, search results for each waiting thread, and the rules; the answer is one JSON object that Consensus carries out.

With a manual send, the queue and the "one call per proposal" rule shrink to the disabled button.

Outcome, if you agree: step 1 becomes "You press Send to LLM in the proposal heading"; automatic calls are dropped. Or should the button be added alongside the automatic trigger rather than replace it?

From Andre in the terminal: the button replaces the existing behavior.

Outcome: step 1 becomes "You press **Send to LLM** in the proposal heading"; nothing else starts a call. Replying, resolving and new threads only leave work waiting, shown in the button's count. The automatic trigger, the queue and the "one call per proposal" rule are dropped; the disabled button takes their place.
